ledger.note: 17 January 1852: the Sand River Convention recognises the Transvaal Boers. 'The South African Republic came into existence on 17 January 1852'; the convention recognised Boer independence north of the Vaal. The region is the 1856 outline without the Lydenburg and Utrecht republics (which are the researcher's reading); the name 'Zuid Afrikaansche Republiek' came in 1853 and was fixed in the 1858 constitution.

region.text: the Republic of Lydenburg (Lijdenburg), around Lydenburg; the circle is the researcher's reading, the page names no boundary

ledger.note: November 1859: the Lydenburg republic joins. The page dates the merger of 'the independent Republics of Lijdenburg and Utrecht' with the ZAR to November 1859. The circle is the researcher's reading of the district.

region.text: the Republic of Utrecht, around Utrecht; the circle is the researcher's reading

ledger.note: November 1859: the Utrecht republic joins (same sentence).

12 April 1877: Britain annexes the Transvaal. 'On 12 April 1877, a proclamation of the annexation of the Transvaal Republic was made in Church Square, Pretoria' (the South African Republic page: 'Annexation of the S. A. Republic to the British Empire', Shepstone). Cliopatria draws the Transvaal inside its British Cape Colony row for 1877-1884, so the counterpart mirrors the british-cape-colony dossier.

December 1880: the Boers rise. 'The Boers revolted on 16 December 1880'; the first clash was the ambush at Bronkhorstspruit on 20 December 1880 (the South African Republic page: the Paardekraal meeting of 13 December 1880 placed authority in Kruger, Joubert and Pretorius, and Heidelberg became the seat).

March 1881: the war ends. After Laing's Nek (28 January), Schuinshoogte (8 February) and Majuba (27 February 1881), Evelyn Wood signed an armistice to end the war on 6 March and 'a peace treaty was signed with Kruger at O'Neil's Cottage on 23 March 1881'.
3 August 1881: the Pretoria Convention ends the occupation. 'The Pretoria Convention was signed on 3 August 1881 and ratified on 25 October'; British troops withdrew.

3 August 1881: the Transvaal under British suzerainty. The British agreed to complete Boer self-government in the Transvaal under British suzerainty, keeping control of external relations, African affairs and native districts.

27 February 1884: the London Convention restores full independence. The ZAR became fully independent on 27 February 1884 (the First Boer War page: 'in 1884, the Pretoria Convention was superseded by the London Convention, which provided for full independence'; the af-07-a Cape dossier notes that Britain kept some control of foreign relations).

region.text: the former Nieuwe Republiek around Vryheid (13,600 km2)

ledger.note: 20 July 1888: the Nieuwe Republiek joins the Transvaal. The republic 'incorporated the former Nieuwe Republiek (Republic of Vryheid) on 20 July 1888'; the New Republic's own page: 'incorporated with the Transvaal Republic on its own request'. Cliopatria dates the addition 1890 and puts it in the wrong place (see the keyframe).

1894: Swaziland becomes a South African Republic protectorate. 'In 1894, a convention placed Swaziland under the South African Republic as a protectorate' (History of Eswatini: signed by the Queen Regent and Swazi Council in December 1894, the Republic's administration under Krogh running to 1899). Cliopatria's 1895 shape draws Swaziland as direct territory.
October 1899: the protectorate lapses with the Second Boer War. The arrangement continued 'until the outbreak of the Second Boer War in October 1899'.

October 1899: the Boer offensive into Natal. 'War was declared on 11 October with a Boer offensive into the British-held Natal and Cape Colony areas'; 'Boer guns began shelling the British camp from the summit of Talana Hill' on 20 October, and the Boers held Dundee. The zone is the Natal ground the colony-of-natal dossier uses (researcher's reading of the town names).

28 February 1900: Ladysmith is relieved. 'Buller's troops marched into Ladysmith on 28 February'; the page gives no date for the Boers' withdrawal from the rest of northern Natal and notes Botha's renewed invasion in September 1901.

ledger.note: 5 June 1900: Pretoria falls. Roberts 'captured Johannesburg on 31 May and the capital of the Transvaal, Pretoria, on 5 June' 1900; 'Roberts declared the war over on 3 September 1900; and the South African Republic was formally annexed' (the Republic's page: a proclamation on 1 September 1900). The republic is drawn occupied, not British, until Vereeniging; the burghers fought on as guerrillas. [Reviewer af-07-b, 2026-10-19] Confidence 2: the page dates the fall of Johannesburg and Pretoria, not the occupation of the whole republic, which the Boers contested to 1902.

wars.name: First Boer War
wars.outcome: Boer victories at Laing's Nek, Schuinshoogte and Majuba; armistice 6 March and peace 23 March 1881; the Pretoria Convention of 3 August 1881 restored Boer self-government under British suzerainty and the London Convention of 27 February 1884 full independence.
wars.note: The counterpart is the british-cape-colony slug only because Cliopatria draws the occupied Transvaal in that row; the belligerent was the British government.

wars.name: Jameson Raid
wars.outcome: 'The British first attacked the ZAR with the December 1895 Jameson Raid,' which failed; no border moved.
wars.note: The page gives the raid in one sentence.

wars.outcome: The Boers invaded Natal and the Cape from 11 October 1899 and besieged Ladysmith to 28 February 1900; Roberts took Johannesburg (31 May) and Pretoria (5 June 1900); the republic was annexed on 3 September 1900 and ended at Vereeniging, 31 May 1902.
wars.note: Mafeking (siege from 13 October 1899) and Kimberley (early November 1899) were besieged outside the republic; they are not zones here.

certainty.note: The pages opened give no boundary terms (not even for the London Convention of 1884), and Cliopatria's outline is a modern-province shape; the Vaal frontier with the Free State and the Natal line are the likely sharp exceptions, but neither is described on a page opened.

notes: Five pages opened (budget up to 5; the Swaziland detail of December 1894 comes from History of Eswatini, read for the swaziland dossier). SETTLED: life 17 January 1852 to 31 May 1902 (Cliopatria 1856-1899, with 1877-1884 inside the British Cape Colony row); the 1877-1884 occupation, contest and vassalage, as the af-07-a Cape dossier expects; the 20 July 1888 incorporation of the Nieuwe Republiek; the Swazi protectorate 1894-1899; the 1900-1902 occupation. NOT SETTLED: (1) Cliopatria's 1890 addition is the mislocated Nieuwe Republiek polygon (Lubombo country, 31.8-32.7E) and two years late; replaced by a 66 km circle at Vryheid from 1888. (2) The Zoutpansberg republic's merger date is not on the page; the 1852-1859 keyframe leaves it inside the republic. The Lydenburg and Utrecht circles are the researcher's reading. (3) The 1856-to-1885 notch (12 cells lost, 4 gained) is unexplained. (4) Boundary changes by treaty with the Swazi, the Zulu, the Free State or Natal (the Wakkerstroom/Klip River arbitration of 1870 in the Free State page) are not on the pages opened; the Transvaal's western frontier (Stellaland, Goshen, the 1884 convention) is not defined on the page, only 'Burghers from Stellaland and Goshen were granted ZAR franchise on 9 May 1887'. (5) Britain's 1877 annexation was the Crown's, not the Cape's; the counterpart british-cape-colony only mirrors Cliopatria's row and the af-07-a dossier. (6) Pretoria 'capital' years before and after the British occupation are bridged; the page gives only Potchefstroom 1858-1860 and Heidelberg 1880-1881. Counterparts needing dossiers: transvaal-colony (successor, 1900-1910), republic-of-lydenburg and republic-of-utrecht (1850s-1859), basutoland, british-colonial-empire exists. Gazetteer names needed: Lydenburg, Utrecht (South Africa), Wakkerstroom, Newcastle (South Africa) and Dundee (South Africa) as places.
